# Dhaga

> Dhaga is a private, open-source personal CRM for founders and relationship-driven professionals: capture meetings, notes, messages, introductions, voice memos, and cards, remember the context, search the network, and follow up at the right time. Open-core: the whole CRM is AGPL and runs fully self-hosted, with a source-available cloud tier.

Dhaga (धागा — Hindi for "thread") is a private relationship memory for founders and other relationship-driven professionals: investors, recruiters, real-estate and financial advisors, consultants, and community builders. Capture a meeting or introduction, write or paste a note or message, forward a contact card, note, or photo through WhatsApp or Telegram, scan a card, clip a page with the extension, or import an address book — Dhaga extracts the people, companies and facts, files them in a private knowledge graph, and answers questions like "who do I know at a fintech in Bangalore?" in plain language. Every AI-derived fact keeps a receipt back to the note it came from, so you can verify it or delete it.

What separates it from Dex, Monica or a notes app: the whole CRM is AGPL-licensed and self-hostable, every external dependency (LLM, web search, embeddings, vector store, messaging) sits behind a swappable provider gateway so you can point it at a local model or your own API key, enrichment only ever runs when you ask for it, and full export always works. The free tier is a complete CRM at $0 forever with unlimited capture and notes. Pro is $10 month-to-month or $8/month billed $96 yearly; the first 500 founding seats can request a $79 first year. Power is shown as a coming-soon plan at $30 monthly or $24/month billed $288 yearly and cannot yet be purchased. Dhaga Cloud is in early access; request access at https://www.dhaga.app/#request-access.

Complete markdown of the 44 pages that answer what Dhaga is, what it does, how it compares, and how to run it yourself — in the same order as the sections of https://www.dhaga.app/llms.txt: start here, then how dhaga compares, then using dhaga, then self-hosting, extending & contributing, then engineering deep dives.

Deliberately excluded to keep this file inside a single model context: the ~153 generated TypeDoc API pages, and the 28 pages listed under `## Optional` in https://www.dhaga.app/llms.txt (the internal build checklist, BRD and manual test plan, plus the per-profession and general networking guides). Fetch any of those individually from the index. Source: https://github.com/anchit2000/dhaga

# Documentation

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/docs

Dhaga is an AI-native, privacy-first personal CRM. Self-host it, extend its providers, or read the product thinking behind it.

**Dhaga** (धागा — "thread") turns every card scan, badge, and voice note into a
private knowledge graph you can search in plain language. It is open-core: the
whole CRM is AGPL and runs fully self-hosted, with a source-available cloud
tier layered on top.

These docs cover running Dhaga yourself, extending it with your own providers,
the generated `@dhaga/core` API reference, and the product thinking behind it.

## Start here

- [Using Dhaga](/docs/guide): The product guide for people using the app — capturing contacts, notes and facts, the graph, and search.
- [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting): Run the full AGPL core yourself — what you get, the hosted-mode switches, and the env var reference.
- [Deploying](/docs/self-hosting/deploy): Vercel, a single server, or Docker — plus the Postgres role and pooling gotchas that matter in hosted mode.
- [Extending Dhaga](/docs/extending): Plug in your own LLM, web search, embeddings, or vector store through the provider gateways.
- [API reference](/docs/api): Generated reference for the public @dhaga/core surface — the gateway interfaces and shared schemas.
- [Development](/docs/development/testing): Deploy it, then click through every shipped feature — the manual verification guide.
- [Contributing](/docs/contributing): Licensing, the branch/PR workflow, the code standards CI enforces, and where to learn more.

## Product & roadmap

- [Product & vision](/docs/product/brd): The full business requirements: problem, competitive landscape, scope, architecture, and cost model.
- [Roadmap & ideas](/docs/roadmap/roadmap): What's shipped, what's in progress, the feature-by-feature build status, and the raw idea backlog.

# I was looking for VCs. They were already in my phone.

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/general/why-i-built-dhaga

Published: 2026-05-20

The night I realized my contacts app remembers nothing — and why I started building the thing that would.

A few months ago I needed to raise money. Not in the abstract, "someday we'll fundraise" way. In the "the runway math has stopped being comfortable and I should probably start talking to people" way.

My first honest thought was: I don't know any VCs.

I sat with that for a bit and felt a little sick about it. You spend years building a thing, you go to the dinners, you shake the hands, and then the one moment you actually need the network you've supposedly been building, your brain returns a flat "nope." I genuinely believed I didn't know anyone who invested in anything.

So I did the thing you do when you're anxious and avoiding the real work. I opened my phone and started scrolling. Contacts first, then WhatsApp, then back to contacts. Thumb moving on autopilot. Names sliding past that meant nothing to me anymore — a first name and a number, no company, no context, no memory of where we'd met or why I'd saved them.

And then, somewhere around the third pass, I started actually reading the names instead of skimming them.

## I was wrong. I knew a lot of them.

There was the guy I met at a conference two years ago who ran a small fund. There was someone from a dinner in — I want to say it was a birthday thing? — who'd said, very casually, over dessert, "let me know if you ever raise, I like getting in early." There was a former colleague who'd mentioned once, almost as an aside, that he does "a bit of angel stuff on the side."

None of that was written down anywhere. It lived entirely in my head, and my head had quietly deleted it. The people were right there in my phone the whole time. What was gone was the *context* — the who-does-what, the who-said-what, the throwaway line at a dinner that was actually an open door.

That's the part that got me. It wasn't that my network was too small. My network was enormous and I'd been walking around convinced it was empty, because the tool I kept it in is basically a phonebook from 1990. Names and numbers. It remembers nothing for you. It has never once, in the entire history of contacts apps, told me anything I didn't already type into it myself.

## The evening I did it by hand

So I spent an evening fixing it manually. This is the unglamorous part.

I made a note on my laptop and I went through the whole list. Every name, one at a time. Trying to remember. Where did I meet this person? What do they do now? Did they ever say anything that sounded like interest? I cross-referenced WhatsApp threads — which are their own special kind of chaos, scattered across a hundred conversations, half of them named "Rahul (conf)" because that's all I knew at the time. I tagged people. I grouped them. I wrote little notes to myself: *"said he angel invests — climate mostly," "wanted to help, follow up," "warm, met twice."*

It took hours. My eyes hurt. But at the end of it I had something real: an actual list of people who invest, and a shorter, better list of people who had, at some point, told me to my face that they'd want in. People I could now actually email. People I could pitch.

And I felt two things at once, really strongly.

The first was relief. The second was a low, specific kind of frustration — because none of that should have taken an evening. The information had always been there. I'd *lived* those conversations. The failure wasn't mine and it wasn't the people's. It was that everything I used to hold onto them was designed to store a phone number and nothing else. All the value — the context, the "he said he'd help" — had to be rebuilt by hand, from memory, at 1am, because no tool had bothered to keep it.

## The thing I couldn't stop thinking about

Here's the insight I keep coming back to, and I don't think it's just me.

Your network is already huge. You are not short on people. You've met thousands of them. The reason it doesn't *feel* huge is that the moment you look away, the context evaporates, and a contact with no context is functionally a stranger. The value was never in collecting people. Anybody can collect people; that's what business cards and LinkedIn connections are. The value is in remembering the stuff *around* the person. What they do. What they said. Why they might matter to you six months from now when the question you're asking has completely changed.

We've all just quietly accepted that this is our job to remember. That it's normal to forget who told you they'd invest. It's not normal. It's a tooling failure we've been apologizing for on the tool's behalf for thirty years.

So that's what I'm building. It's called Dhaga — it means "thread." The idea is simple and it comes straight out of that evening: you capture people and little notes as you go — after the dinner, after the call, whenever — and instead of dumping them into a dead list, it quietly turns them into a private map of who you know and what you know about them. And then, when you need it, you just ask. In plain English. "Who do I know who invests in climate?" "Who did I meet who offered to help?"

One question. Not an afternoon of scrolling.

I'm building it because I needed it and it didn't exist, which is the only reason I trust myself to build anything. I still think about that night — the specific stupidity of sitting there convinced I knew no one, while a folder full of people who'd literally offered to help sat glowing in my hand.

If you've ever had that feeling — the certainty that your network is useless, right up until the moment you actually look — then you already understand the whole thing, and I'd love for you to come along.

---

# Roadmap

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/docs/roadmap/roadmap

What's shipped, what's in progress, and what's next — a contributor-facing summary derived from the build checklist and the BRD.

Dhaga is built in the open. This page tracks what's shipped, what's in
progress, and what's next — derived from the full
[build checklist](/docs/roadmap/checklist) and the
[business requirements doc](/docs/product/brd), which has the complete rationale behind
each phase. This page is a summary for contributors and prospective
self-hosters; check those two docs for the exact feature-by-feature detail.

See the [build timeline](/docs/roadmap/timeline) for how this was built, day by day, from 2 July 2026.

Status legend:

- **Shipped** — built, verified (typecheck/lint/build/tests + a manual
  click-through), and live in the codebase.
- **In progress** — code exists and passes automated checks, but is missing
  a manual verification step (a live API key, a physical device, a real
  purchase) or a final polish pass.
- **Planned** — not started.

## MVP: the core loop

The BRD's MVP is one loop: *scan → auto-group by event → voice note → entity
extraction → natural-language search → AI follow-up draft.* The original plan
was to build this mobile-first; in practice the team built the full loop on
the **web app first** (faster iteration, no app-store review cycle), then
started on the native mobile app. So MVP status splits in two:

| # | Feature | Web | Mobile |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | Card scan → structured contact | **Shipped** (photo upload → vision parse → edit-before-save) | In progress — camera → on-device OCR → Haiku parse spike is built but not yet verified on a real Android/iPhone |
| M2 | Auto event grouping | **Shipped** (create, rename, merge, active-event default) | Planned — time + location clustering |
| M3 | Voice + text notes | **Shipped** (Dhaga Voice — on-device Moonshine transcription, WebGPU — + transcript) | Planned — on-device transcription |
| M4 | Entity extraction (facts, relationships, follow-ups) | **Shipped** | Shares the same backend once mobile capture lands |
| M5 | Knowledge graph v0 | **Shipped** (contact connections, graph browser, tags) | Shares the same backend |
| M6 | Natural-language search | **Shipped** (keyword + semantic + AI answer with receipts) | Shares the same backend |
| M7 | AI follow-up drafts | **Shipped** (draft, edit, copy) — one acceptance check (that every draft cites a note-derived fact) still needs a manual pass with a live API key | Shares the same backend |
| M8 | Local-first storage + export | **Shipped on web** (Postgres, CSV/vCard/JSON export) | Planned — on-device SQLite as source of truth, full offline mode |

Every AI-derived fact carries a receipt back to the note it came from, and
"forget this person" cascades across contacts, notes, facts, edges, and
embeddings — both true today, not aspirational.

## v1.1 — Capture everywhere

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Web quick-add (paste email signature / free text / article) | **Shipped** |
| Browser extension (Chrome/Edge, one-click capture + "save this article to X") | **Shipped** — Chrome Web Store listing is packaged and ready; publishing itself needs a manual reviewer demo account and the one-time developer registration fee |
| LinkedIn Connections CSV import | **Shipped** |
| User-triggered public-web enrichment | **Shipped** |
| Badge scanning | Planned |
| Email-forwarding ingestion | Planned |

## v1.2 — Proactive intelligence

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Keep-in-touch reminders (Home reach-out feed) | **Shipped** |
| Post-event digest email | **Shipped** |
| On-demand pre-meeting brief | **Shipped** (graph-only; not yet calendar-triggered) |
| Job-change detection (web-search based) | In progress — built, needs a manual pass with live API keys |
| Opt-in news watchlist per contact | In progress — built, needs a manual pass with live API keys |
| Relationship-decay ("going quiet") detection | In progress — built, needs a manual click-through |
| Relationship-strength scoring | In progress — built, needs a manual click-through |
| Calendar integration → auto-pushed briefs | Planned |

## v1.3 — Graph power

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Warm-path finding ("who can intro me to X?") | **Shipped** |
| Second-degree ("nearby in your network") suggestions | **Shipped** |
| Relationship timeline view | **Shipped** |
| Watch app / widgets | Planned |

## v1.4 — Ecosystem

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Outbound webhooks | **Shipped** |
| Telegram capture + Q&A bot | **Shipped** |
| Salesforce / HubSpot / Notion sync | Planned |
| WhatsApp capture | **Shipped** |
| LinkedIn QR formats | Planned |
| Gmail/Outlook interaction sync (opt-in) | Planned |

## v2.0 — Teams

Shared org graph, cross-team "who knows whom," SSO, per-seat billing. This is
the primary planned revenue line and hasn't been started — everything shipped
so far is single-user.

## Self-hosting & launch readiness

- The AGPL core (accounts, capture, notes, graph, search, drafts, export,
  Telegram, the extension API) runs fully self-hosted with **zero**
  dependency on the proprietary `packages/ee` module — see
  [Self-hosting](/docs/self-hosting).
- `docker compose up` — the `Dockerfile` and `compose.yml` exist and look
  complete on read-through, but haven't been run end-to-end yet. Treat as
  in progress until someone confirms a clean run.
- Dhaga Cloud (hosted multi-tenancy, early-access gate, admin panel, Stripe
  billing) is code-complete and passes automated checks but is still
  pre-launch: no live Stripe products, no manual click-through in a browser
  yet, nothing pushed to production.

## Contributing

Good first issues are labeled `good-first-issue` on GitHub — small,
self-contained pieces of the checklist above that don't require a live API
key, a physical device, or deep familiarity with the codebase. If something
in this roadmap interests you and isn't yet labeled, open an issue and ask;
we're happy to scope it down together.

# Dhaga vs Dex: Private CRM vs Auto-Sync CRM

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-dex

Published: 2026-07-24

Dex vs Dhaga compared — automatic LinkedIn/email sync vs open-source privacy and a free tier that actually works. Which personal CRM fits?

**The short version**

Dex is the category-leading personal CRM, and its whole superpower is automatic capture — it syncs your Gmail, calendar, and LinkedIn for you and even detects job changes. Dhaga doesn't do live sync yet; it's the open-source, self-hostable, privacy-first option with a free tier that's actually usable. So "Dhaga vs Dex" really comes down to one honest question: do you want zero-effort auto-sync in a polished cloud app, or do you want to own your data outright? Pick by that, not by feature counts.

If you've been shopping for a personal CRM, you've hit Dex (getdex.com). It's the most well-known dedicated one for a reason: roughly 30,000+ users, a clean product, and a pitch that lands — "one place for your relationships," built for people, not a sales pipeline. If you're weighing it against an open-source challenger, this is the honest Dex-vs-Dhaga breakdown, written by someone who builds the challenger. I'll be upfront about where Dex plainly wins, because it wins a lot.

The short version of the tension: Dex is a managed cloud product that captures your network *for* you. Dhaga is a private, open-source graph you feed and own. Those are two genuinely different bets, and the right one depends entirely on what you value.

## The core difference: automatic capture vs. private ownership

Everything else is downstream of this one split.

**Dex's bet is convenience.** It plugs into the accounts where your relationships already live — Gmail/Outlook (two-way email sync), Google Calendar, LinkedIn — and quietly builds your CRM without you typing much at all. Its most impressive trick: automatic **job-change detection**, so when a contact moves companies, Dex notices and nudges you to reach out. That is a real, mature, hard-to-build feature, and it's the beating heart of the product.

**Dhaga's bet is ownership.** It's an AI-native personal CRM built privacy-first: you capture people as you go, those notes become a private knowledge graph you query in plain English, and the whole thing is open-source (AGPL) and self-hostable. The tradeoff is the honest headline of this whole comparison: **Dhaga has no live email, calendar, or LinkedIn sync today.** You get contacts in through manual add, a LinkedIn Connections CSV export, a browser extension, a paste of an email signature, or a Telegram bot — not an ambient background feed.

So if the single most important thing to you is that your CRM fills itself, stop reading and get Dex. That's not false modesty; it's the truth, and it's what Dex is best in the world at.

## Where Dex wins (and it's not close on these)

Being fair here matters, because Dex is the incumbent and it earned the position. Where it's clearly ahead of Dhaga right now:

- **Automatic capture from email, LinkedIn, and calendar.** The whole value prop, and it's mature. Two-way Gmail/Outlook sync, calendar sync, LinkedIn auto-sync (up to 9,000 connections on the top plan), iMessage/social sync, two-way phone-contact sync. Dhaga has none of these as live sync.
- **Automatic job-change detection + reach-out notifications.** Dhaga has no live equivalent shipping today.
- **Mature, polished native mobile + desktop.** Dex has real iOS and Android apps (with business-card scan and AI voice notes on mobile) and a desktop app. Dhaga's mobile surface today is an installable PWA — the native apps are still in progress.
- **AI pre-meeting briefs from your calendar.** Dex Copilot / Ask Dex does natural-language recall and CRUD ("who did I meet at the Google event in product?"), plus calendar-aware meeting prep and daily digests.
- **A shipped MCP server + agent skill, today.** You can point Claude or ChatGPT at Dex and have it operate the CRM. Dhaga now ships an MCP server too — `/api/mcp`, ten tools, and the read half costs no AI credits — so what's left of the gap here is Dex's packaged agent skill and its longer mileage, not the connection itself. (Dhaga's write tools are additive only: no delete, no merge, no bulk actions.)
- **Power-user plumbing.** Mail merge, Zapier, and a public API on the Professional plan.
- **Brand, reliability, and a big user base.** ~30,000+ users and years of polish. A newer open-source project can't hand you that on day one.

Dex is also privacy-*respecting* in the ways that matter to most people: it's supported by subscriptions rather than ads, says it never sells your data, and gives you full export and delete. The one thing it can't offer — because it would break its own model — is self-hosting.

## Where Dhaga wins

Now the other side, honestly. These are real advantages, and most of them are exactly the things Dex *structurally can't* match without abandoning its cloud model.

- **Open-source and self-hostable.** Dhaga is AGPL with a one-command `docker compose up`. Your entire relationship graph can live on infrastructure you control — inside India if data residency matters to you. Dex is closed-source central cloud; there's no self-host, and there never can be without changing what Dex is.
- **A free tier that's actually usable.** This is the sharpest contrast. Dex's free plan exists but is deliberately thin: unlimited contacts, but *basic reminders only* — no integrations, no AI, and no mobile app. Dhaga's free tier is a real working tool: manual capture, notes, follow-up reminders, warm-path finding, and search across your own graph, at zero cloud-AI cost. (Dhaga's AI features — natural-language recall, card and voice capture, drafting — are the paid tier, around $8/month. Cloud AI is opt-in and metered, never always-on.)
- **Fact-level provenance and cascade delete.** Every AI-derived fact in Dhaga keeps a receipt — the note it came from. Delete that note and its derived facts, edges, and embeddings go with it. "Forget this person" cascades completely. That's a privacy invariant built into the schema, not a settings toggle.
- **Warm-intro pathfinding at zero AI cost.** Dhaga walks your own graph — shared companies, events, and relationships — to find the shortest warm path to someone you want to reach. It's local graph traversal, so it costs nothing and reveals nothing to a model.
- **Cheap capture rails with no integration or subscription.** A Telegram bot, a paste box, a LinkedIn CSV import, a browser extension. None of it requires wiring up an OAuth integration or paying for a tier.
- **India + founder/operator/VC positioning.** Built for people who live on warm intros and read pricing in rupees, not just US knowledge workers.

## Feature by feature

Here's the head-to-head. Read the highlighted rows in both directions — the bottom row is where Dex wins outright, and it's the most important row for a lot of people.

A couple of honest footnotes on that table. Dhaga's natural-language recall and card/voice capture live in the paid tier, not the free one — the free tier is manual capture plus keyword search of your own graph. And "Partial" on Dex's connection graph is fair: Dex maps your contacts and surfaces mutuals, but explicit warm-intro pathfinding is a Dhaga strength.

## Pricing, read honestly

Dex's real prices: **Free** ($0, basic reminders only). **Premium** ~$12/month billed annually ($144/year) or $20/month monthly — this is the tier that unlocks LinkedIn, Gmail, calendar, AI, and mobile. **Professional** ~$20/month annually adds LinkedIn up to 9,000 connections, Outlook, mail merge, Zapier, and the API. There's a 7-day trial and up to a 50% student discount.

For an Indian reader, the Premium tier is roughly ₹12,000 a year — and note that the *useful* Dex (integrations + AI + mobile) starts at Premium, not free. Dhaga's free tier is a genuinely usable manual CRM at ₹0, with AI on a ~$8/month Pro plan if and when you want it. If you're comparing total cost of ownership across the field, our roundup of the [best personal CRM apps in India](/blog/guides/best-personal-crm-apps-india) puts both in context with Monica, Mesh, and Notion.

## Which should you choose?

This one maps cleanly. No hand-waving:

| If you… | Choose |
|---|---|
| Want zero-effort auto-capture from email/LinkedIn/calendar | **Dex** |
| Want polished native mobile + desktop today | **Dex** |
| Will happily pay ~$12/mo for a managed product that "just works" | **Dex** |
| Require privacy, data ownership, or self-hosting | **Dhaga** |
| Prefer open-source you can audit and run yourself | **Dhaga** |
| Want a genuinely useful *free* manual tier (AI only if you opt in) | **Dhaga** |
| Are a founder/operator/VC in India living on warm intros | **Dhaga** |

> The real question isn't which tool has more features. It's whether you'd rather your CRM fill itself in someone else's cloud, or stay entirely yours on infrastructure you control.

If you want the deeper why-you-own-it argument, [Personal CRM vs LinkedIn](/blog/guides/personal-crm-vs-linkedin) covers why a public directory can't be your private memory. And if what you actually want is the open-source lane specifically, [Dhaga vs Monica](/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-monica) compares the two AGPL options head-to-head.

## The takeaway

Dex is the safer, more finished product, and if automatic capture is the feature you'd trade everything else for, it's the right call — a Dex alternative only makes sense if you're optimizing for something Dex doesn't give you. But if you searched for a getdex alternative because you want ownership, an open-source codebase, self-hosting, and a free tier that isn't crippled, that's a different tool with a different bet.

That tool is [Dhaga](/) — free to start, open-source to inspect, and yours to run. Just go in clear-eyed: you're trading Dex's automatic sync for control, not getting both. Today, that's the honest deal.

# Dhaga vs Louisa AI: Personal vs Enterprise Graph

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-louisa

Published: 2026-07-24

Louisa AI vs Dhaga — enterprise, firm-owned relationship intelligence vs a private personal CRM you own. Different buyers, compared honestly.

**The short version**

Dhaga vs Louisa isn't a feature fight — it's two different products for two different buyers. **Louisa AI** is enterprise relationship intelligence: a firm buys it so a whole team can mine its collective network, and the graph belongs to the firm. **Dhaga** is a personal CRM: you install it, the graph is *yours*, and it goes with you when you change jobs. If you're an individual, Louisa was never built for you. If you're a revenue team at a bank or fund, Dhaga isn't trying to be your rollout.

You probably landed here after searching for a **Louisa AI alternative**, or trying to figure out where Dhaga fits next to it. The honest answer up front: they overlap on the words — both say "**relationship intelligence**," both let you ask "**who knows whom**" in plain English — and diverge on almost everything that decides which one you should actually pay for.

The single question that sorts it is *whose graph is it?* Louisa builds a graph that belongs to a firm. Dhaga builds a graph that belongs to a person. Get that straight and the rest of this comparison falls into place.

## Two products wearing the same words

"Relationship intelligence" has become a category label that hides more than it reveals. Both tools promise to turn scattered relationship data into something you can query. The difference is the *subject* of the graph.

Louisa's subject is the firm. It pools every partner's, investor's, and associate's network into one org-wide graph, then answers questions like "which of my colleagues can get me to this CFO?" That's enormously valuable — and it only works because there are colleagues to pool. A single user with no team gets a fraction of the point.

Dhaga's subject is you. It maps the people *you* know from your own notes and captures, and answers "who do I know who invests in climate?" from your private memory. There are no colleagues to borrow from — and for an individual, that's the feature, not the limitation. Your graph isn't diluted by, or dependent on, anyone else's.

## What Louisa AI actually is

Credit where due: Louisa (louisa.ai) is a serious enterprise product. It spun out of Goldman Sachs in 2023, founded by Rohan Doctor, on roughly a $5M seed. Its marketing cites "150,000+ users," though that figure isn't independently verified. It sells "deal intelligence for relationship-driven firms" — investment banks, private equity, law firms, consultancies — the places where knowing the right person before Tuesday is worth real money.

The product is three parts:

- **Louisa for CRM** — auto-cleaning, entity resolution, and dedupe on your existing CRM data.
- **Louisa for Revenue** — daily briefs of cross-sell and origination opportunities, each with a warm path, supporting signals, and an estimated deal value.
- **Louisa Connects** — auto-maps alumni and partner networks and surfaces connection paths across the firm.

It auto-ingests from Salesforce, Dynamics, DealCloud, HubSpot, Affinity, and Backstop, plus Outlook/Gmail, calendars, LinkedIn, alumni databases, and Snowflake/Databricks. It monitors millions of news articles a day for signals, and deploys in about four weeks. On the AI side it ships an MCP connector into Claude Desktop, Claude Code, and Cursor — its own demo query is "Who at our firm can introduce me to Meridian's CFO before Tuesday?", returning ranked colleagues with interaction history.

On privacy it's enterprise-grade: SOC 2 Type II, GDPR/CCPA, read-only ingestion, and a stated policy that your data never leaves your environment, is never shared, and is never used to train external models. But note the ownership nuance that matters most to an individual reader: that data is the *firm's*. Louisa is not open-source (there's a local-or-cloud MCP option, not a verified self-host product), it has no business-card scan or voice capture, and its iOS app is built for enterprise use. There's no India slant, and — critically — **the graph disappears when you leave the firm.** It's a company asset, not a personal one.

There are no public prices; every call to action is "Book a conversation." A single third-party review *reports* — not confirmed by Louisa — figures around $50/user/mo for individuals, $800/team/mo at the SMB tier, and custom enterprise pricing, with no free tier. Treat those numbers as folklore until Louisa publishes its own.

## Where they diverge

A few of those cells need honest footnotes. Dhaga's **natural-language recall is a paid feature** — the free tier is manual capture and search; asking your graph questions in plain English sits on the paid Pro plan. A Dhaga **team/org graph is on the roadmap, not shipped** — today Dhaga knows *your* contacts, not your colleagues'. And "own your data personally" is a check for Dhaga specifically *because* it's self-hostable and open-source: keep the graph on your own machine and no employer, and no vendor, can take it away.

## Where Louisa wins (honestly)

If you're a team, Louisa does things Dhaga simply doesn't:

- **An org-wide graph.** It pools every colleague's network into one map. Dhaga only knows the people *you* know. For a firm trying to find who among two hundred partners can reach a target, that pooling is the whole product.
- **Zero-touch ingestion.** It pulls from email, calendar, CRM, and LinkedIn automatically, with entity resolution, so nobody has to manually capture anything. Dhaga is capture-first: you feed it.
- **Proactive deal signals at scale.** Daily briefs backed by news monitoring across millions of articles, with estimated deal value attached. That's a revenue engine, not a memory aid.
- **Deep enterprise integrations** into DealCloud, Backstop, Snowflake, Databricks, and the rest — the plumbing a large firm already runs on.
- **Enterprise trust and scale.** SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, a Goldman Sachs pedigree, and an architecture built to hold millions of relationships across a whole organization.

None of that is faint praise. If the job is *arm a revenue team*, Louisa is aimed squarely at it.

## Where Dhaga wins

For an individual, the ledger flips:

- **It's built for one person.** Louisa needs a firm and colleagues to be useful; Dhaga is useful the moment you capture your second contact. No team required.
- **You own the data — permanently.** Dhaga is open-source (AGPL core) and self-hostable. Your graph lives where you put it and survives every job change. Louisa's graph is the employer's and is gone when you walk out.
- **A free tier and a ~$8/mo Pro plan** — versus no free tier and a reported per-seat price roughly 6x higher. You can start at zero and stay there if all you need is manual capture.
- **No rollout, no IT, no sales cycle.** There's no four-week deployment and no "book a conversation." You sign up and go.
- **Capture from anywhere.** Business-card scan, voice notes, web quick-add, a browser extension, and a Telegram bot — the messy, on-the-go ways an individual actually collects people. Louisa has none of these; it ingests from corporate systems instead.
- **Receipts and clean deletion.** Every AI-derived fact keeps a link to the note it came from, and deleting a contact cascades fully through notes, facts, edges, and embeddings. Your data leaves as cleanly as it arrived.

The one claim Dhaga *won't* make: that its relationship graph is unique. Plenty of tools, Louisa included, map connections. Dhaga's difference is that the map is private, built from your own notes, self-hostable, and yours.

## Who should choose which

This is the rare comparison where the right answer is almost never "it depends" — it's "who are you?"

**Choose Louisa** if you're a revenue team at a relationship-driven firm — a bank, a PE shop, a consultancy, a law firm — with budget, a tolerance for a four-week rollout, and a real need to mine your colleagues' collective network for origination. That's exactly the buyer it was built for.

**Choose Dhaga** if you're an individual — a founder, an operator, a solo VC, especially one living on warm intros in the India ecosystem — who wants a private, self-hostable **personal CRM** they actually own, with a free manual tier and cheap paid AI, and no employer, org, or procurement process in the loop.

Different buyers, plainly. If you want to see how Dhaga stacks up against the *other* personal CRM most individuals consider, read [Dhaga vs Dex](/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-dex). And if what you're really after is finding the shortest path to someone specific, the mechanics are in [warm introductions and mutual connections](/blog/guides/warm-introductions-mutual-connections).

## Takeaway

Louisa AI and Dhaga both sell "relationship intelligence," but they answer to different masters. Louisa's graph belongs to a firm and pays off when a team mines it together; Dhaga's graph belongs to you and pays off the moment you need to remember who you know. If your network is a company asset, Louisa is the serious tool. If your network is *yours* — and you want it to stay yours through every job you'll ever have — that's the whole reason [Dhaga](/) exists.

---

# Dhaga vs Monica: Open-Source Personal CRM Compared

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-monica

Published: 2026-07-24

Monica vs Dhaga — two open-source, self-hostable personal CRMs compared on AI, capture, and features. Which should you self-host?

**The short version**

Monica and Dhaga are the two serious open-source, self-hostable personal CRMs — same license (AGPL), opposite bets. Monica is mature, community-loved, and built for the breadth of your personal life (gifts, journal, debts, reminders), with **no AI, on purpose**. Dhaga is newer and AI-native: card/voice capture, a private knowledge graph, natural-language recall, and warm-intro pathfinding. Pick Monica for a proven manual relationship journal; pick Dhaga if you want AI to do the capturing and remembering. Both let you self-host and own your data.

If you've decided your relationship data belongs on infrastructure you control, the open-source shortlist is genuinely short. In the **open source personal CRM** niche, two names come up again and again: Monica — the incumbent — and Dhaga, the newer AI-native option. This guide is the honest **dhaga vs monica** comparison: where each one wins, where each one loses, and which one you should actually self-host.

Full disclosure up front: I build Dhaga. So I'm going to be scrupulous about Monica's strengths, because a comparison that trashes a genuinely excellent tool isn't worth reading. Monica is very good. For a lot of people it's the right answer.

## Two open-source twins, opposite bets

Both tools rhyme on the fundamentals, which is exactly why people compare them:

- **Both are AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable.** You can `docker compose up` either one, point it at your own database, and never send your contacts to anyone else's cloud.
- **Both are personal CRMs, not sales CRMs.** Neither is a deal pipeline. Both are private memory about the people in your life.
- **Both have a free path.** Monica is free to self-host (its hosted tier starts at 10 contacts free); Dhaga's core is free and open, with a free tier you run yourself.

Then they diverge, hard. **Monica** (MonicaHQ) launched around 2017 on PHP/Laravel and spent nearly a decade getting deep at one thing: manually logging the texture of your personal relationships. Its README says it plainly — there is no AI, by design. **Dhaga** started from the opposite premise: that typing everything by hand is the failure mode, and AI should do the capture and recall for you. One tool bet on **breadth without AI**; the other bet on **AI plus a graph**. Almost every real difference below flows from that one split.

## Where Monica is genuinely better

Let me state Monica's wins without softening them, because they're real and they matter.

**Maturity and community.** Monica has roughly eight years of polish and one of the larger communities in open-source personal software. That shows up as stability, documentation, translations, and a plugin ecosystem Dhaga simply hasn't had time to grow.

**Breadth of personal-life logging.** This is Monica's real moat, and it's substantial. Monica tracks gifts (given and received), a journal with mood, debts you owe or are owed, activities you did together, pets, tasks, calls, documents, and multiple separate vaults. If your goal is a rich, hand-kept diary of the people you love — birthdays, the book you lent them, the gift idea you had in June — Monica has years of thoughtful features Dhaga has not built and isn't trying to.

**A flat, proven price.** Monica's hosted tier is a simple $9/month or $90/year, unlimited contacts, no metering. Predictability is a feature.

**"No AI" is itself a feature.** For a privacy purist, Monica's zero-AI stance is a selling point, not a gap. Nothing gets inferred, nothing gets metered, nothing leaves the box unless you typed it. That's a legitimate thing to want, and Dhaga — which does call a model for its AI features — can't offer that particular kind of quiet.

> If you want a proven, self-hostable journal of your relationships and you'd rather no model ever touch your notes, this comparison has a short answer: use Monica.

Monica's one honest gap is capture and recall speed — everything goes in by hand, comes back out by browsing, and there's no shipped production mobile app today. A ground-up rewrite (codenamed Chandler) is in beta, so the project is far from stalled.

## Where Dhaga pulls ahead

Dhaga's whole reason to exist is the thing Monica deliberately skipped: getting information *in* and *back out* without manual labor.

**AI-native capture.** Scan a business card with your phone, dictate a voice note in the browser, paste an email signature, or clip a page with the extension — Dhaga extracts the structured fields for you to review, instead of asking you to type name / company / title into a form. (Card scan and browser voice capture are built and shipped on the web app today.)

**A private knowledge graph, not a flat list.** Your notes get turned into structured facts and typed relationships — works-at, knows, met-at — so your contacts form a graph you can traverse, not rows you scroll.

**Natural-language recall.** Ask *"who do I know who invests in climate?"* in plain English and get an answer built from **your own** notes, each with a receipt pointing back to the note it came from. This is the feature Monica has no equivalent for — and it's a **monica personal crm alternative**'s clearest reason to exist. One caveat, stated plainly: Dhaga's AI recall is a **paid** capability. The free tier is manual entry with **zero cloud AI** — closer to Monica's model than to Dhaga's paid one — and self-hosters bring their own API key.

**Warm-intro pathfinding.** Because the graph is real, Dhaga can trace a path from you to someone you want to reach through shared mutuals. Monica maps direct relationships; it doesn't do multi-hop introduction paths. (This one runs on local graph traversal, so it costs no AI spend at all.)

**Receipts and cascade delete.** Every AI-derived fact stores the note it came from, and deleting a contact cascades through notes, facts, edges, and embeddings — so "forget this person" actually forgets them. For an AI product, that provenance is the privacy floor.

**Native mobile is in progress.** An early Expo build (iOS + Android) exists but isn't the finished app yet — so on mobile, honestly, both projects are still catching up.

Here's the whole thing on one grid.

Read that last row carefully — it's the honest one. Monica wins breadth; Dhaga wins AI and graph. Neither column is a knock on the other tool; they set out to build different things.

## The pricing math

Both are free to self-host, which is the comparison that actually matters for a **self-hosted personal crm**. On the hosted side:

| | Monica | Dhaga |
|---|---|---|
| Self-host | Free (AGPL) | Free (AGPL core) |
| Hosted free tier | 10 contacts | Free tier (manual, no cloud AI) |
| Hosted paid | $9/mo flat, unlimited | Paid tier unlocks AI (capture, recall, drafts) |
| AI metering | None (no AI) | Yes — AI is the metered, paid layer |

The philosophies show through even here. Monica charges a flat fee for a feature set with no variable inference cost behind it. Dhaga meters AI because AI has a real per-call cost — and keeps a genuinely usable free tier that doesn't touch a model at all. If you never want to pay for or think about inference, that's a point for Monica.

## Who should choose which

**Choose Monica if** you want a proven, free, self-hostable journal of your personal relationships; you value the gifts / journal / debts / activities breadth; and you either distrust AI or simply don't want it near your notes. Monica is the mature, honest, no-surprises choice, and any **monica crm alternative** has to earn its place against roughly eight years of polish.

**Choose Dhaga if** you want AI to do the capturing and the remembering — card and voice capture in, natural-language recall out — plus warm-intro pathfinding across your graph; you're a founder, operator, or investor (especially in India) who lives on warm intros; you want native mobile on the roadmap; and you still want open-source and self-host as the non-negotiable floor.

If you're weighing self-hosting more broadly, our guide on [open-source & self-hosted CRM for startups](/blog/guides/open-source-self-hosted-crm-startups) goes deeper on the ops trade-offs. Comparing hosted tools too? The [best personal CRM apps in India](/blog/guides/best-personal-crm-apps-india) roundup covers the proprietary field, and [Dhaga vs Dex](/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-dex) pits Dhaga against the best-known closed-source AI option.

## The takeaway

Monica and Dhaga are two open-source twins that made opposite bets. Monica bet on breadth without AI and won a mature, beloved tool for hand-keeping the details of your personal life. Dhaga bet on AI plus a graph and built capture, recall, and warm-intro pathfinding on top of the same open-source, self-hostable foundation. There's no loser here — just two honest answers to "what should remembering people feel like."

If the AI-native, graph-native side is what you've been missing, take a look at [Dhaga](/). And if it's the manual, journal-rich side you want, Monica is genuinely excellent — go use it.

# Dhaga vs OpenVC: Warm Intros vs Investor Database

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-openvc

Published: 2026-07-24

OpenVC vs Dhaga — a fundraising investor database vs a private relationship graph you own. Complementary tools for founders raising a round.

**The short version**

OpenVC and Dhaga get compared because both live near a fundraise — but they're different categories of tool. OpenVC is a fundraising platform: a curated database of thousands of investors you can filter, pitch, and track through a raise. Dhaga is a private personal CRM: a relationship graph of everyone *you already know*, kept as searchable memory you own. One helps you find and reach investors; the other helps you remember every relationship for life. If you're raising, the honest answer is usually "use both."

If you searched *dhaga vs openvc* — or landed here looking for an *OpenVC alternative* — you're probably mid-raise, staring at your runway math, trying to figure out which tool actually solves your problem. Here's the most useful thing I can tell you up front: these two barely overlap. Comparing them feature-for-feature is a little like comparing a directory of investors to your own memory of the people you've met. Both are about relationships. They do opposite jobs.

This guide lays out what each one is genuinely good at, where each falls short, and why — for a founder raising a round in India or anywhere else — the smart move is usually to run both rather than pick one.

## They're not the same category

**OpenVC** (openvc.app) is a fundraising platform. Its own tagline is "raise capital for your startup from ~16,600 investors," and that's exactly the job. It gives founders a curated, verified investor database you can search by stage, sector, geography, and check size, then reach out and track through your raise. It's founder-facing and, by their own numbers, used by around 40,000 founders. OpenVC exists to help you **find investors** for the round you're running *right now*.

**Dhaga** is a personal CRM — a private knowledge graph of the people you already know. You capture contacts and context from anywhere (a business-card scan, a voice note after a coffee, a web quick-add, a browser extension, your own LinkedIn connections export), and it stitches those notes into a graph you can query and keep for years. It has no external investor directory and never will — it only knows people you've actually met. Dhaga exists to help you **remember** relationships across every raise, every hire, every role.

So the real question was never "which one wins." It's "which job are you doing?" — and often the answer is both. OpenVC sources people you *don't* know. Dhaga remembers the people you *do*.

## What OpenVC does well

A comparison that trashes the other tool is worthless, so let me be straight about OpenVC's strengths — several of them are things a personal CRM structurally cannot do:

- **A curated, verified investor database.** Roughly 16,000+ investor profiles, filterable by geography, check size, stage, industry, and even reply rate. This is cold-investor *discovery* — sourcing people you don't know yet — and it's the thing Dhaga fundamentally can't offer.
- **In-platform outreach.** Submit your deck to investors who accept inbound, and run cold outreach without leaving the tool.
- **A native fundraising CRM.** A proper raise pipeline to track which investor sits at which stage of your process.
- **Deck hosting + engagement analytics.** Host your pitch deck and see opens, time-per-slide, which slide people stopped on, and where they viewed it from — real signal during a live raise.
- **An AI pitch-deck reviewer.** Slide-by-slide feedback on your deck.
- **Intro Finder (Premium).** Connects your Gmail and LinkedIn to surface mutual-connection **warm intros to investors** specifically.
- **Strong India coverage.** Dedicated India / Bengaluru / Delhi investor pages — which matters a lot if you're raising here.
- **A genuinely generous free plan.** Around 90% of the features — database search, the fundraising CRM, deck hosting, and one AI deck review — are free. Premium ($99/mo or $299/yr) adds 5 outreaches a day, 10 filters, Intro Finder, unlimited AI reviews, plus masterclass and partner perks.

One honest note on OpenVC's AI: it's deck review and investor matching. It is *not* natural-language recall over your own notes and relationships. Different AI, different job — which is exactly the seam between these two tools.

## Dhaga and OpenVC, side by side

Read the matrix as two columns that mostly *don't* compete. OpenVC owns the fundraising rows — the external database, the deck pipeline, the outreach — and Dhaga can't touch them. Dhaga owns the memory rows — a private graph of everyone you know, plain-English recall of your own notes, and the ability to host it yourself. The two rows where both light up (warm-intro paths, "own your data") are where the honest nuance lives.

Two clarifications so the table doesn't oversell either side. First, Dhaga's **natural-language recall** — asking "which investors did I meet who write pre-seed cheques?" in plain English — is a paid feature; the manual system underneath it (notes, facts, follow-ups, reminders, warm-path finding) works free with zero cloud AI. Second, the two OpenVC cells marked as a dash — *self-host / open-source* and *own your data* — reflect that we found **no evidence** of an open-source repo, a self-host option, or documented data export for OpenVC. Treat those as *not verified* rather than a hard "impossible": it's a closed hosted SaaS as far as we could confirm, and if data portability matters to you, ask them directly.

## Where Dhaga is the better tool

If your job is remembering relationships for the long run — not sourcing a cold investor list — Dhaga does things OpenVC isn't built for:

- **A private graph across *all* your relationships, not just investors.** OpenVC is scoped to the raise. Dhaga holds customers, hires, mentors, ex-colleagues, and the friend who casually mentioned they "do a bit of angel stuff" — the whole network, in one place you can query. Most warm intros you'll ever get come from people who were never on any investor list.
- **Ongoing relationship memory instead of transactional history.** OpenVC is built around *this* raise. Dhaga is built to outlive it: capture what an investor actually said, log the objection as its own fact with a receipt back to the note it came from, set a keep-in-touch cadence so the relationship doesn't quietly decay after the round closes. The investors who pass this time are your warm list for the next one — but only if something remembers them.
- **Multi-surface capture.** Scan a badge at a demo day, dictate a voice note in the taxi home, quick-add from the browser, bulk-import your LinkedIn connections — every path lands in the same graph.
- **You own the data — you can self-host it.** This is the sharpest contrast. OpenVC's Intro Finder works by ingesting your Gmail and LinkedIn into its cloud. Dhaga is open-source (AGPL core) and self-hostable — a `docker compose up` and your relationship graph runs on your own infrastructure. A sensitive raise doesn't have to live on someone else's servers.

The flip side, stated plainly: Dhaga only knows people you already know. It has no cold-investor discovery, no deck hosting, no slide analytics, and no raise pipeline. If your problem is "I don't know enough investors," Dhaga is the wrong tool for *that* half of the problem.

## Use both: OpenVC finds the investor, Dhaga remembers the relationship

The cleanest way to think about it is a handoff. OpenVC is brilliant at the front of the funnel — discovering and reaching investors you don't yet know. Dhaga is built for everything downstream — turning those investors (and everyone else you meet) into durable, private memory you can reuse for years.

In practice: you use OpenVC to build a target list and get in front of partners you've never met. The moment a conversation happens, you capture it in Dhaga — who they are, what they said, the objection they raised, the follow-up you promised — and Dhaga starts tracing warm-intro paths from *your own* network to the funds on your list, because a two-hop warm intro still beats a cold submission. (We go deep on that in [warm introductions and mutual connections](/blog/guides/warm-introductions-mutual-connections).) OpenVC's day-one value is that it works with *zero* of your own data. Dhaga's value compounds precisely *because* it's your data, accumulating across every raise and role.

## So which should you pick?

A simple rule:

- **Choose OpenVC when the job is "raise *this* round."** You need to discover and reach cold investors, host and track a deck, and run a fundraise pipeline. That's its whole reason to exist, and the free plan makes it a low-risk yes.
- **Choose Dhaga when the job is "own my relationship intelligence for life."** You want a private, self-hostable **investor CRM** — and contact CRM — that remembers every conversation, surfaces warm paths, and answers questions in your own words, long after any single raise is over.
- **Use both, and it's not redundant.** OpenVC to find and reach investors; Dhaga as the durable private graph of everyone you meet along the way — those investors included — so next time you're raising, the wall of *"I don't know any VCs"* simply isn't there. For the discipline of running that relationship layer through a raise, see [investor relationship management for startups](/blog/guides/investor-relationship-management-startups).

## The takeaway

*Dhaga vs OpenVC* was always the wrong framing. OpenVC is a fundraising platform that finds and reaches investors you don't know; Dhaga is a personal CRM that remembers the ones you do — privately, queryably, and on infrastructure you can own. They meet at exactly one point: the warm intro. Use OpenVC to fill the top of your raise, and let [Dhaga](/) turn every person you meet along the way into a private graph you'll still have when the next round starts.

---

# Dhaga vs YourPond: Which Personal CRM Remembers?

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-yourpond

Published: 2026-07-24

YourPond vs Dhaga — a polished iOS relationship app vs an open-source, AI-native personal CRM you own. Which remembers your network best?

**The short version**

YourPond is a polished, 5.0-rated iOS app built to make you "the friend who remembers" — warm profiles, a multi-generational family tree, a map of where people live, and an analytics dashboard. Dhaga is an open-source, AI-native personal CRM you can self-host and query in plain English. If you want a finished consumer contact book for your personal life on an iPhone, pick YourPond. If you want to own your data and *ask* your network questions, pick Dhaga.

Every personal CRM app sells the same promise: remember the people you meet, so you're not the one who forgets a name, a birthday, or the fact that someone offered to help. YourPond and Dhaga both make that promise. They just answer the question — which personal CRM actually *remembers*? — in two very different ways.

One is a closed, genuinely beautiful iOS app that remembers *for* you. The other is open-source infrastructure that remembers *with* you, on hardware you can control. This is an honest Dhaga vs YourPond comparison, written by someone who builds one of them — so I'll be upfront about where Dhaga wins and where YourPond plainly does it better today.

## What YourPond gets right

Let's start with credit, because YourPond (yourpond.io, by Lilypad Labs) earns it. Its tagline — "Be the friend who remembers" — is aimed squarely at thoughtful individuals keeping up with friends, family, and personal life, with a secondary pitch to founders. It carries a 5.0 App Store rating, and the product feels like it.

The rich contact profiles go well beyond name and number: how you met, birthdays, education, preferences, pets, even "moments" you want to hold onto. Its signature features are the ones most personal CRM apps don't bother with — a relationship graph plus a genuine **multi-generational family tree** that models in-laws, step-relations, and inferred links, a **map** of where your contacts live, and a finished relationship **analytics dashboard**. It surfaces mutual connections and introduction suggestions (including warm-intro paths to investors on its founders page), and it nudges you with reminders for birthdays, anniversaries, and thank-you notes. You can capture by natural-language text, and there's **voice entry on iOS**. Pricing is a simple flat Pro tier — no AI metering to think about.

That is a lot of finished, warm, consumer-grade polish. If your goal is a beautiful holiday-card list with gift preferences and thank-you nudges, YourPond is a strong pick, and Dhaga is honestly behind it on several of these: Dhaga's native mobile app is still early, and it has no family-tree modeling, no map view, and no polished analytics dashboard. Credit where it's due.

## Where the two apps diverge

Here's the head-to-head on the axes that separate these two tools rather than the ones they share.

Both apps map your connections and suggest warm intros, so don't read that row as a knock on either — a connection graph is table stakes now. The real forks are two: what the AI is *for*, and who can read your data.

## Fork one — AI for entry, or AI for recall

This is the most important distinction in the whole comparison, and it's easy to miss because both apps say "AI."

YourPond uses AI for contact **entry**. Paste a bio or a signature and it extracts the fields for you — a genuinely useful Pro feature that saves typing. But that's where the intelligence stops. There's no evidence YourPond lets you *ask* your contacts anything in natural language; you can't query "who do I know in fintech who mentioned they angel invest?" and get an answer back. The AI fills the form; it doesn't answer the question.

Dhaga's entire thesis is the second half. Capture a person however is fastest, and Dhaga turns those notes into a private knowledge graph you query in plain English — recall, not just entry. That's the part that decides whether a personal CRM app actually earns the word "remembers." One caveat, stated plainly: Dhaga's natural-language recall is the paid tier. The free tier covers manual capture, notes, and organization; cloud AI (the "ask your network" part, plus follow-up drafts) is metered and paid, around $8/month.

## Fork two — who can read your data

YourPond is privacy-*conscious*, and it's important to be precise here rather than sloppy. Sensitive fields are encrypted at rest, and the company is clear: no ads, no data sales, no AI training on your data. That's a better posture than most consumer apps.

But it is explicitly **not** zero-knowledge, and YourPond says so plainly — the vendor *can* read your data. It's a closed-source cloud app with no self-host option, built on the usual stack (Clerk for auth, Stripe for billing, Anthropic for extraction, which holds typed text up to 30 days). Export exists but is **manual** — you email them to get it. None of that makes YourPond "not private"; it makes it a trusted-cloud model, where your relationship history lives on infrastructure the vendor controls and can see.

Dhaga sits on the other side of that fork by design. It's open-source (AGPL) and self-hostable with a single `docker compose up`, so if you run it yourself there is no vendor in the loop to read your data. Export is self-serve — CSV, vCard, or a full JSON dump, any time, no email required. Every AI-derived fact keeps a receipt pointing back to the note it came from, and deleting a note tombstones the facts it produced, so "forget this person" actually cascades. The hosted tier is a convenience where you trust open, auditable code rather than a black box; the guarantee that the vendor can't read your data comes from self-hosting. If you're specifically hunting for a **YourPond alternative** whose privacy model is ownership rather than trust, that's the whole reason Dhaga exists.

## Capture and platforms

The two apps also draw people in through very different doors.

| | Dhaga | YourPond |
|---|---|---|
| Text / paste (AI extract) | Yes | Yes (Pro) |
| Voice capture | Web app | iOS only |
| Business-card scan | Yes | No |
| Browser extension | Yes | No |
| Chat capture | Telegram bot | No |
| Bulk import | CSV, vCard, connectors | LinkedIn / Google / CSV / Excel (Pro) |
| Platforms | Web + installable PWA (native mobile early) | iOS-first, limited web, no Android |

YourPond's capture is text, iOS voice, and bulk import — polished, but narrower, and firmly iOS-first with no Android and no India presence. Dhaga spreads capture across more channels: a business-card scanner, voice notes on the web app, a quick paste, a browser extension, and even a Telegram bot, plus CSV and vCard import. It runs on the web today with an installable PWA on Android and iPhone, while the native mobile apps are still in progress — so YourPond wins the "finished native iPhone experience," and Dhaga wins the "works on Android and the web, and captures from more places."

On price: YourPond is free permanently up to 25 contacts, then $10/month or $100/year for unlimited plus AI entry, import, and analytics. Dhaga's free tier has no contact cap but no cloud AI; Pro is around $8/month for metered AI recall and drafts, and because it's open-source, self-hosting removes the per-seat cost entirely.

## Who should choose which

> The best personal CRM isn't the one with the longest feature list — it's the one whose data model and privacy posture you can live with for years. Pick the fork, then pick the app.

Map it to how you actually work:

| If you… | Choose |
|---|---|
| Are an iPhone user who wants a beautiful, finished contact book for friends and family | YourPond |
| Love family-tree modeling, a map of where people live, and a relationship-analytics dashboard | YourPond |
| Are fine with a closed cloud app that can read your (encrypted) data | YourPond |
| Want open-source, self-host, and data you actually own | Dhaga |
| Want to *ask* your network questions in plain English | Dhaga |
| Need multi-channel capture, Android + web, and a founder / operator / VC (India) slant | Dhaga |

Neither answer is wrong. They're built for different people, and the honest test is which set of tradeoffs you'd still be happy with in two years of feeding it your relationships.

## Takeaway

YourPond is the better *finished consumer product* right now — a warm, polished, 5.0-rated iOS app that will make you the friend who remembers birthdays. Dhaga is the better *foundation to own* — open-source, self-hostable, multi-channel capture, and natural-language recall over a private knowledge graph, with the tradeoff that native mobile is still early and the smartest AI is the paid tier.

If you want to see how both stack up against the wider field, [Best Personal CRM Apps in India (2026)](/blog/guides/best-personal-crm-apps-india) runs the same honest lens across six tools, and [Dhaga vs Dex](/blog/guides/dhaga-vs-dex) covers the other polished-cloud comparison people ask about.

If the open-source, own-your-data, ask-it-in-plain-English bundle is what you're after, [Dhaga](/) is free to start and open to inspect.

# Personal CRM vs LinkedIn: Which Keeps Your Network?

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/blog/guides/personal-crm-vs-linkedin

Published: 2026-07-24

Why LinkedIn forgets your connections, and how a personal CRM keeps every conversation and follow-up.

**The short version**

LinkedIn is a public directory optimized for LinkedIn — it's brilliant for reach and discovery, but it forgets the private context that actually makes a network useful: who you really met, what you discussed, what you promised to follow up on. A personal CRM keeps that context as memory you own. The honest answer to "personal CRM vs LinkedIn" is: use both. LinkedIn for reach, a personal CRM for relationships.

You have 2,000 connections on LinkedIn. Quick — who among them raises seed rounds in fintech? Who did you meet at that Bengaluru conference in March? Who said, over coffee, "ping me when you're hiring a design lead"?

LinkedIn can't tell you. It knows you're *connected* to these people. It doesn't know why you'd want to talk to them today. That gap — between having a connection and remembering what the connection is *for* — is the whole reason a personal CRM exists, and it's why so many founders and operators end up rebuilding their network by hand at 1am before a fundraise.

This isn't a "quit LinkedIn" post. LinkedIn does a few things better than any personal CRM ever will. But it was never built to be your memory, and treating it like one is why your network feels smaller than it is.

## LinkedIn is a directory, not a memory

Here's the thing worth saying plainly: **LinkedIn is not a CRM.** It's a directory — a public, searchable index of professional profiles, optimized to keep you scrolling a feed and coming back tomorrow. That's a legitimate product. It's just a different product from the one that remembers your relationships.

A directory answers "who is this person, publicly?" A CRM answers "what is my relationship with this person, privately?" Those are different questions, and LinkedIn is structurally built to answer only the first one.

Watch what LinkedIn actually optimizes for. The feed. Engagement. Reach. Premium upsells. Every design decision points outward — toward more content, more connections, more time on platform. None of it points inward, toward *your* context. LinkedIn's search indexes public profile fields — titles, companies, skills people chose to list — not the throwaway line at dinner that was actually an open door.

> LinkedIn remembers that you're connected. It does not remember *why*.

And when you do try to store context on the platform, it slips away. Private notes and tags on a connection — the "how you met," the little reminders — used to live in the free product. LinkedIn moved them into Sales Navigator, its paid sales tool. So the one feature that made LinkedIn feel like a contact manager is now a subscription upsell aimed at quota-carrying salespeople, not a founder trying to keep track of who they know.

## Why LinkedIn "forgets" your connections

It's tempting to say LinkedIn forgets your network. More precisely: it never tried to remember it in the first place. A few structural reasons why:

- **Context isn't a field.** LinkedIn stores what people publish about themselves. It has no place for what *you* observed — that this person is between jobs, that they're raising, that they offered to intro you to their old CTO.
- **The graph is public and shared.** Your "connection" to someone is symmetric and visible. There's no private layer where your candid notes ("great engineer, terrible at replying to email") can live safely.
- **The feed buries people.** Discovery on LinkedIn is whoever the algorithm surfaced today, not whoever you actually need. The people most relevant to your current question are usually the ones the feed never shows you.
- **Follow-up is on you.** There are no keep-in-touch reminders. If you meant to reconnect with someone in three months, LinkedIn will not remind you. It will show you their promotion nine months later, in your feed, framed as content.

None of this is a bug. It's what a public professional directory is supposed to do. The mistake is expecting it to double as your private relationship memory. For the practical mechanics of not dropping people, our guide on [how to follow up after a networking event](/blog/guides/how-to-follow-up-after-a-networking-event) goes deeper.

## What LinkedIn is genuinely great at

Being fair matters here, because the answer isn't "personal CRM wins." LinkedIn is best-in-class at things a personal CRM simply can't do:

- **Public reach and discovery.** You can find almost any professional on earth, see their background, and reach out cold. No private CRM built from your own contacts can match a global, public index.
- **Being found.** Recruiters, investors, and potential customers find *you* through LinkedIn. Inbound is a real channel, and it only works because the directory is public.
- **Social proof.** Mutual connections, endorsements, a visible track record — LinkedIn is where people go to check if you're legit before they take the meeting.
- **Low-friction connecting.** One tap to connect, and you're loosely linked forever. That's a genuinely useful weak-tie network.

If you're building a professional network from scratch — especially early in a career or a move to a new city — LinkedIn's reach is unbeatable. We cover that side of the equation in [how to build a professional network in India](/blog/guides/how-to-build-professional-network-india). The point isn't that LinkedIn is bad. It's that reach and memory are two different jobs, and LinkedIn only does the first one.

## What a personal CRM keeps that LinkedIn drops

A personal CRM is the private half of the equation: relationship memory you own. Not a public profile, not a feed — a place where the context lives. Private notes on the people you meet. Reminders to reach back out before a relationship goes cold. The ability to ask, in plain English, "who do I know who invests in climate?" and get an answer from *your own* history instead of a public search.

Here's the honest comparison, feature by feature:

Read that bottom row carefully: **LinkedIn wins public discovery, outright.** A personal CRM built from your own contacts can't and shouldn't try to be a global directory. But look at the rows above it — that's the private context LinkedIn either charges for, exports in a stripped-down form, or doesn't keep at all. That column is exactly what people mean when they go looking for a LinkedIn contacts management alternative: somewhere to hold the notes and reminders LinkedIn never made room for.

The "keep in touch reminders" row is the one I'd underline. Relationships decay silently. A personal CRM can nudge you before a warm contact goes cold; LinkedIn can only show you their news after the fact.

## You don't own your LinkedIn network

This is the part founders underrate until it bites them. Your LinkedIn connections are not really *yours* — they're a graph that LinkedIn hosts, governs, and can gate at any time.

You can export a data archive, yes. But it's deliberately thin: for years LinkedIn stripped email addresses out of the connections export unless the other person opted in. You get names and headlines, not the relationship. And the account itself lives at LinkedIn's discretion — one policy change, one suspension, one pivot in what the feed rewards, and the network you spent a decade building shifts under you. You're renting.

A personal CRM inverts that. The data is yours: full export to CSV, vCard, or a complete JSON dump, any time, no lock-in. If you'd rather not trust anyone else's server at all, an open-source, self-hostable one lets you run the whole thing on your own infrastructure — the network is genuinely yours, on your terms. For a broader look at the open-source options, see [the best personal CRM apps in India](/blog/guides/best-personal-crm-apps-india).

A quick nuance, because "private LinkedIn" is a real category now: tools like **Mesh** (formerly Clay) explicitly pitch themselves as a private version of LinkedIn — auto-building your network from your inbox and social accounts, and even overlaying mutual connections on LinkedIn itself. They genuinely close the *memory* gap LinkedIn leaves open. What they don't close is the *ownership* gap: Mesh is a closed, cloud-hosted product (now owned by Automattic), so your relationship graph still lives on someone else's server. If "private" just means "not public," that's enough. If "private" means "on infrastructure I control," only an open-source, self-hostable option actually gets you there.

## Use both: LinkedIn for reach, a personal CRM for relationships

The framing that actually works: **LinkedIn is your front door; a personal CRM is your memory.** They're complementary, not competitors.

Use LinkedIn to be discovered, to research people before a meeting, to send the first connection request, to catch a job change in the feed. Then, the moment a connection becomes a real relationship — you had the call, they made the offer, you owe them a follow-up — that context belongs somewhere private that will actually keep it.

That's the job [Dhaga](/) is built for, and the reason it exists as a personal CRM rather than another social network. You capture people as you go — a business-card scan after an event, a quick voice note in the cab, a paste from an email signature, one tap from the browser extension. Those notes quietly become a private knowledge graph you can question in plain English: *"Who did I meet at the fintech dinner who mentioned they were hiring?"* You get reminders before warm contacts go cold. And because it's privacy-first and open-source — self-hostable, with your data exportable at any time — none of it depends on an algorithm deciding what you get to remember.

For founders and operators in India who live on warm intros, that split is the whole game: LinkedIn gets you in the room, and a personal CRM makes sure that six months later you still remember who was in it, what they said, and why they matter now. That's why "better than LinkedIn for keeping in touch" isn't really a competition — LinkedIn was never trying to keep in touch for you.

## The takeaway

Don't ask which one to use. Ask which one to use *for what*. LinkedIn is the best public directory ever built — keep it for reach, discovery, and inbound. But stop asking it to be your memory, because it was never designed to be, and every relationship you let it quietly drop is a warm intro you'll be rebuilding by hand later.

A personal CRM keeps the half LinkedIn forgets. If you've ever been convinced your network was empty right up until the moment you actually looked, that's the half worth owning.

[See how Dhaga keeps your network →](/)

# Using Dhaga

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/docs/guide

A task-oriented tour of the Dhaga app — capture people anywhere, turn notes into a private knowledge graph, and query it in plain language.

**Dhaga** turns everyone you meet into a private knowledge graph you own. You
capture a person once — from a card photo, a pasted email signature, a voice
note — and Dhaga keeps the source as a receipt, extracts the facts, and wires
them into a graph you can search, ask questions of, and explore visually.

This guide walks through the app the way you actually use it. Each page is a
short "how to" for one part of the product.

## Your daily briefing

`/app` opens on the Home briefing — the short list of **threads to pull
today**: people worth reaching out to now, follow-ups you set, and the people
you touched most recently. Each row has a one-tap **Reached out** button so the
list stays honest. Once your graph isn't empty, a **graph at a glance** strip
renders beneath the briefing — quick counts of People, Companies, Notes, Facts,
Relationships, Events, Open follow-ups, and Entities. When AI extraction needs a
decision from you, a **Confirmations** preview tile surfaces the count of pending
confirmations waiting on your yes/no. The capture dock sits at
the bottom of every screen —
**Voice**, **Camera**, **Upload**, and **Capture** — so you can add someone the
moment you meet them.

![Dhaga Home showing a "To confirm" tile of pending AI confirmations, the daily briefing list of people to reach out to, a follow-ups panel, recent people, and the bottom capture dock](/docs/guide/home.png)

## The sections

- [Capturing people](/docs/guide/capturing-people): Quick-add by paste, card scan, voice, camera, or file — plus the review step and manual add.
- [Messaging capture (WhatsApp & Telegram)](/docs/guide/messaging-capture): Forward a contact card, note, or photo to the Dhaga bot on WhatsApp or Telegram, reply DONE, and it saves into your graph.
- [Importing contacts](/docs/guide/importing-contacts): Bring in an existing address book — a .vcf or CSV file, a one-click Google or Outlook connect, or your phone's contacts.
- [Syncing with your phone](/docs/guide/syncing-your-phone): Keep your phone's address book and Dhaga in step both ways — a three-way merge that never silently overwrites, with your notes and facts kept out of it.
- [Bulk actions & merging](/docs/guide/merging-and-bulk-actions): Select many people at once to merge, tag, star, add to a company, or forget — and let Dhaga surface likely duplicates to clean up.
- [Notes & facts](/docs/guide/notes-and-facts): Add notes by typing, by voice, or by photo; facts get extracted automatically, each with a source receipt.
- [Calendar & reminders](/docs/guide/calendar): See your follow-ups on a full-screen calendar, drag to reschedule, and stay nudged by the nav bell and a daily reminder email.
- [Confirmations](/docs/guide/confirmations): The inbox where ambiguous AI extractions wait for your call — confirm or dismiss, and nothing changes your graph until you do.
- [Enrich from the web](/docs/guide/enrich-from-web): One button to search the public web for a person's footprint — cited, saved as a deletable note.
- [Groups & events](/docs/guide/groups-and-events): Group the people you met somewhere into an event, add them in a row, and email a digest.
- [Exploring the graph](/docs/guide/exploring-the-graph): Your whole network on one canvas — warm-path intros, node panels, layers, and controls.
- [Search & Ask Dhaga](/docs/guide/search-and-ask): The ⌘K palette: filter by name, fact, or note, or ask a natural-language question with receipts.
- [Connect an AI assistant (MCP)](/docs/guide/mcp): Point Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor at your graph over MCP — six read tools with receipts, four additive write tools, and no credits for the reading.
- [Custom entities](/docs/guide/entities): Non-person nodes — gyms, schools, projects — that connect the people in your graph.
- [Companies](/docs/guide/companies): View, create, rename, delete, and merge the companies in your graph — with duplicate detection — from their own page.
- [Share & invite](/docs/guide/share-and-invite): Post a contact-free Wrapped card of your networking, and invite friends for a free month of Pro on both sides.
- [Settings & import](/docs/guide/settings): Profile, appearance (theme + font), billing, 2FA, calendar, suggestions, voice, API keys, and bringing in your existing contacts.
- [AI credits](/docs/guide/ai-credits): What's left this month, what each AI action costs, and exactly where the credits you spent went.

Self-hosting or wiring up providers instead? Start at the
[documentation home](/docs).

# AI credits

Source: https://www.dhaga.app/docs/guide/ai-credits

The Credits tab in Settings — how many AI credits you have left this month, what each action costs, and exactly where the ones you spent went.
